name: Grace Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the coal handling plant at a big open-cut coal mine. I run the stacker-reclaimer, which is a huge machine on rails that builds the coal into long stockpiles and then digs it back out onto the conveyor for the trains. I've been there just under two years, and before that I was a bank teller for sixteen years until our branch closed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you go from a bank to a coal plant?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, the money. The branch shut because everyone does their banking on their phones now, and the mine was hiring and paid nearly double. My husband Mark is an electrician and he'd done contract work at the plant, so he told me to apply. I'm still learning the stockpile patterns, and I mess up the blending sometimes, but the guys are patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that sounds pretty normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that, then. Probably a joke in the crib room about how the robots are on strike. I wouldn't make a big deal of it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still think about coal. AI or not, everyone knows coal's got a limited run. So I'd be relieved about the AI part and still be watching the coal price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, learn the blending properly and try for the control room upgrade next year. We'd keep the three months saved and add a bit. Mark would keep picking up his contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've already lost one job to technology, at the bank. Does that make you trust the AI Plateau picture less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. The bank didn't change overnight, it was ten years of small things, new machines, then apps. So a plateau might just be the slow part before the next step. I'd keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra time if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably finally get my forklift ticket, which they want in the plant. And go to Emma's netball games without checking my roster first, that'd be nice.

S0.say: I'd say 'well, that's that, then' and joke that the robots are on strike. I wouldn't make a big deal of it online.
S0.think: I'd be relieved about AI but still watching the coal price, because coal has a limited run anyway. A plateau might just be the slow part before the next step.
S0.do: Keeps her job, learns the blending properly and aims for the control room upgrade next year. Adds a little to the three months saved and gets a forklift ticket.
S0.quote: The bank didn't change overnight, it was ten years of small things, new machines, then apps.
S0.fieldNote: Grace has lived through slow automation at the bank, so she reads the plateau as a possible pause rather than an end. Coal's own decline is always in the back of her mind, separate from AI. She's practical and unexcited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one, I can picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so get the training sorted early. I'd say that at work and to my mum, who worries. No point shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the plant would go mostly remote, because some plants already run from a control room in the city. If I'm in that room, I'm fine. If I'm not, I'm out, and I'm junior, so it could go either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch which of the operators got moved into the control room first and how they went. Once it looked solid, I'd ask for the training, maybe six months in. I'd use the AI tools the way I do now, to help me read the manuals and write up shift reports, and we'd hold off on replacing the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like at the bank when the first rumour went around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at the bank after that first rumour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It took four years before the branch actually closed. In that time, three people moved to head office and two of us got packages. I took mine and came here, which turned out alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if jobs shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody really, it's how things go. The company should be fair about it, and the government should help with training. I don't think there's a villain here.

S1.say: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so get training sorted early. No point shouting about it.
S1.think: I think the plant would go mostly remote and I'd either be in the control room or out. Being junior, it could go either way.
S1.do: Watches which operators move to the control room first, then asks for the training about six months in. Uses AI tools for manuals and shift reports, and delays replacing the car.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like when the first rumour went round at the bank.
S1.quote: I don't think there's a villain here.
S1.fieldNote: Grace's bank story is her map: rumour, years of waiting, then packages. She sees no villain, only a process that should be fair. She'd follow others into the control room once it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fast. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to move fast and keep people afloat, whatever it costs. And companies shouldn't get to pocket all the savings. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the plant would be one of the first places to go fully automatic, because it's already halfway there. I'd lose my job within a year or so. We'd have Mark's income, which matters a lot, but not if robots do wiring too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back right away, no holiday, no new car, groceries on a list. I'd ask Mark about working as his offsider, his apprentice basically, because a sparky's van needs two people for a lot of jobs. And I'd look at what the government offers, without being too proud to take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be doing sums in my head constantly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change, compared to longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years isn't enough to finish an electrical apprenticeship, that's four years. So I'd just be a helper. With two years you grab whatever's closest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Emma and Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emma's fifteen and already asks about uni. I'd tell her to keep going with school but to pick something with people in it. Jonas is twelve, I'd just tell him Mum might work with Dad for a while, he'd think that's fun.

S2.say: I'd say the government must move fast to keep people afloat, and companies shouldn't pocket all the savings. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it.
S2.think: I think the plant would be among the first to go fully automatic and I'd be out within a year. My husband's income matters a lot, unless robots do wiring too.
S2.do: Cuts the holiday, the new car and grocery spending right away. Starts working as her husband's electrical offsider and applies for government support without pride getting in the way.
S2.feel: Anxious, doing sums in her head constantly.
S2.quote: With two years you grab whatever's closest.
S2.fieldNote: Grace's partner's trade gives her a cushion and a fallback that many miners lack, which keeps her from the top of the scale. She's realistic that two years means helper work, not an apprenticeship. She speaks plainly to her kids and nudges her daughter toward people-facing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them properly. Fund apprenticeships for adults, not just kids. I'd say that at work and to our local member if she asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is long enough to get most of the way through an electrical apprenticeship as an adult. Working with Mark, I'd be qualified around when the robots arrive. It's not a guarantee, but it's a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the plant for the first year to keep the money coming and save to five months. Then I'd start an adult apprenticeship with Mark, which means a pay cut, so the savings matter. I'd use AI tools to help with the theory, the way I already do with the manuals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. More focused than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be taking a pay cut with a mortgage and two kids. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tightly. Apprentice pay for an adult is better than for a teenager, but it's still a big drop. We'd rent out the granny flat, that's maybe two hundred a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind about this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mark's work started drying up too. Then there's no point both of us being in the same trade. I'd watch his bookings, they tell you a lot.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years, so fund apprenticeships for adults, not just kids. I'd tell my local member if she asked.
S3.think: I think five years is long enough to get most of the way through an adult electrical apprenticeship with my husband. It's not guaranteed, but it's a trade.
S3.do: Stays at the plant for the first year and saves to five months, then starts an adult apprenticeship with her husband despite the pay cut. Rents out the granny flat and uses AI tools for the theory.
S3.feel: Uneasy but focused, with a plan.
S3.quote: I'd watch his bookings, they tell you a lot.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Grace's fallback into a real retraining plan, timed against the arrival of AGI. She's specific about money: adult apprentice pay, the granny flat rent. She watches her husband's bookings as an early warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be in my fifties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair runway and nobody should waste it. People should start thinking now about what they'll do. That's about it, I'm not one for big speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, coal might be winding down by then anyway, so it's a double clock. I'd be fifty-three, Emma would be through uni, Jonas would be finishing school. I think we'd be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the stacker for a few years and build up savings to six months. Around year three or four, once I'd seen how the first adult apprentices went, I'd start mine. And I'd put a bit extra on the mortgage each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because of coal, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a double clock. Which one worries you more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coal, if I'm honest. AGI in ten years is a maybe. Coal closing is something they talk about every year at the toolbox meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything at home change with ten years to plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We might stay put rather than move to the bigger house we've been eyeing. Less debt seems smart either way.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a fair runway and nobody should waste it. People should start thinking now about what they'll do.
S4.think: I think coal might be winding down anyway, so it's a double clock, but at fifty-three with the kids grown I think we'd be okay.
S4.do: Stays on the stacker for a few years and builds savings to six months, paying a bit extra on the mortgage. Starts an adult apprenticeship around year three or four, and drops plans for a bigger house.
S4.feel: Uneasy, more about coal than robots.
S4.quote: AGI in ten years is a maybe. Coal closing is something they talk about every year at the toolbox meeting.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Grace's worry shifts from AI to coal itself. She'd take the same apprenticeship route but wait to see how others go first. She drops the bigger house to keep debt down.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is funded adult apprenticeships with a decent wage, so people like me can afford to retrain with a mortgage. And honest notice from the company.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like to have lost a job to technology once already. You don't get angry the second time, you just start planning. I've done it before, I can do it again, I just want a bit of warning.

headlineQuote: You don't get angry the second time, you just start planning.
portrait: Grace Schmidt is 43 and runs a stacker-reclaimer in the coal handling plant of an open-cut coal mine, almost two years in after her bank branch closed. She's pragmatic and steady, sees no villain in automation, and uses AI tools now and then for manuals and reports. She expects the plant to go remote under Steady Disruption and would follow others into the control room. With AGI, her fallback is her electrician husband's business, as a helper in two years or an adult apprentice with five or ten. Over the long run she worries about coal more than robots.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there'd be no time to finish an apprenticeship.
whatWouldHelp: Funded adult apprenticeships with a decent wage so people with mortgages can retrain, and honest notice from the company.
